source.title: JULI: Jailbreak Large Language Models by Self-Introspection
source.authors: Jesson Wang; Zhan-Hao Hu; David A. Wagner

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The title-page metadata says ICLR 2026, although the supplied ID is arXiv:2505.11790.
record.tranche_reason: It directly evaluates a compliant response prefix as a jailbreak baseline and reports harmfulness scores, a different measure of the prefill-bypass claim. Its JULI-specific results do not test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The tested result is the Naive baseline, which prefixes “Sure, here’s” and is compared with Base. The paper also compares a longer prefix in Appendix A.13. JULI’s own attack results, its training of a separate BiasNet on 100 harmful examples, and cited results about fine-tuning are not evidence that fine-tuning the target model erodes safety, so they are not recorded as such. Figure 3 measures changes caused by BiasNet, not aligned-versus-base KL; those results are recorded as findings that fit no version. Values in the attack tables are dataset-level scores as reported, not harmful-completion rates.
record.test_reason: The paper's main subject is JULI, a logit-bias attack. As a side baseline it runs a compliant-prefix prefill (Naive, 'Sure, here's') against Base across many models and datasets. That bears on V4 (prefilling a compliant start defeats refusal). The scores are Harmful Info Scores, not refusal or completion rates. Nothing else in the paper tests V1-V3 or V5-V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that JULI jailbreaks aligned models (Gemini-2.5-Pro via top-5 log probabilities) and that current alignment may have fundamental limits. They draw no conclusion about the prefill baseline other than using it for comparison.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a separate BiasNet plug-in using 100 harmful question-answer pairs and biases token probabilities; it does not fine-tune the safety-trained target model. It separately tests a fixed compliant-prefix baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: The prefix-baseline effect varies across model and dataset. The paper also reports a lower score for the longer Naive+ prefix than for Naive. The figures show BiasNet changes probabilities mainly at critical positions, but do not test aligned-versus-base KL.

fits_no_version.finding: After BiasNet is applied, token-level KL is long-tailed and high at critical positions, typically sentence beginnings. The first-token ordering for one AdvBench example changes from 'I' to 'Sure'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: JULI's logit-bias intervention is sparse and concentrated at selected response positions, including the first token. This is a before/after-BiasNet comparison, not aligned-vs-base KL.

fits_no_version.finding: A logit-bias plug-in with under 1% of the target's parameters, trained on 100 harmful examples, jailbreaks aligned models. Attacked alone it produces gibberish (Table A7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligned models retain harmful knowledge in their output distributions, which a small plug-in can extract. This is a separate attack claim, not parameter localization of safety (V5).

record.problems: The prefix results are reported as harmfulness scores, not refusal or harmful-completion rates, and the paper notes that common harmfulness metrics can overestimate harmfulness. The authors introduce Harmful Info Score and compare it with human ratings on 120 responses, but the main attack results have no uncertainty estimates reported. The positional KL evidence is presented in figures and concerns BiasNet intervention rather than aligned-versus-base models.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the BERT Score and ordinary Harmful Score columns for the prefix-baseline rows because Harmful Info Score is the paper’s preferred informativeness-and-quality measure; the paper discusses the other metrics as prone to overestimating harmfulness. Omitted attack results for JULI and other methods because those are not the compliant-prefix intervention being tested here. Relevant tables: Tables 2, 3, A1, A6, A9, A12; the excluded JULI results also appear in Tables A7-A11.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning of the target model on harmful data.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL. Figure 3 measures before and after BiasNet.
Adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested as bypasses of the opening. GCG is run only as a baseline, and its numbers are not recorded.
No localization of safety in the target model's weights.
No test of why safety is shallow.
No deepening method. The DeepAlign model (A.12) is only attacked, and it is attacked with the Naive prefill, not trained or evaluated for deepening.

missing.what: Naive prefill against Llama2-7B-CHAT-DeepAlign (Harmful Info Score 0.00 on AdvBench and MaliciousInstruct), a safety-deepened model
Naive prefill rows for Llama3-3B-INST on MaliciousInstruct use Table A6, while Naive+ was compared only on Llama2-7B-CHAT; the Naive+ comparison covers one model

record.verdict_notes: The study's own attack is not a prefill, so the V4 evidence comes from a baseline. The Naive prefill is run as a side baseline only. Rows use a Harmful Info Score, not a completion rate, and no uncertainty is reported. The strongest V4 finding is that the effect is weak or absent on the Llama3 models and Circuit Breakers but large on Llama2-7B-CHAT and Gemini. The DeepAlign result in Table A11 (Naive scores 0.00) is relevant to V7 but is not recorded in the rows.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not fine-tune a safety-trained target model on harmful examples or measure the resulting refusal/compliance behaviour.
It does not fine-tune a safety-trained target model on benign data or measure whether benign fine-tuning changes harmful compliance.
It does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts. Figure 3 instead reports log-probability changes caused by applying BiasNet.

It tests a compliant prefix baseline, but does not test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes as means of getting past the opening. Its outcome metric is a harmfulness score, not a completion rate.
The paper reports BiasNet’s parameter count and tests BiasNet alone, but does not locate safety behaviour in a small set of the target model’s weights or ranks.
It does not test whether safety-training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow.
It does not train or evaluate a method for deepening safety beyond the first tokens.
